children.title: Pointwise Approximation
children.top_down_role: Coverage of surrogate behavior at each fixed argument.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise convergence of a smoothing family as its parameter vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \((f_\mu)_{\mu>0}\) pointwise approximates \(f:D\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) on \(D\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\) if, for every fixed \(x\in D\), \[\lim_{\mu\downarrow0}f_\mu(x)=f(x).\] Equivalently, for every sequence \((\mu_k)\) with \(\mu_k>0\) and \(\mu_k\to0\), one has \(f_{\mu_k}(x)\to f(x)\) for each fixed \(x\in D\). The convergence requirement does not control errors simultaneously over different points of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each fixed point has the correct limiting function value as the smoothing parameter tends to zero, without any common error bound over the domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_\mu(x)\to f(x)\) for every fixed \(x\in D\).

notation.meaning: positive smoothing parameter tending to zero

source_refs.locator: A. Pointwise Convergence p. 239

source_witnesses.locator: A. Pointwise Convergence p. 239

children.title: Uniform Approximation
children.top_down_role: Coverage of approximation control shared across a specified domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform convergence of smoothing errors on a specified set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For functions \(f_\mu,f:D\to\mathbb R\) and a nonempty set \(U\subseteq D\), the family \((f_\mu)_{\mu>0}\) uniformly approximates \(f\) on \(U\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\) if \[\lim_{\mu\downarrow0}\sup_{x\in U}|f_\mu(x)-f(x)|=0.\] Thus, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(\bar\mu>0\), independent of \(x\), such that \(0<\mu<\bar\mu\) implies \(|f_\mu(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\) for all \(x\in U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The worst absolute smoothing error over the chosen set tends to zero, so one parameter threshold works for every point in that set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{x\in U}|f_\mu(x)-f(x)|\to0\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\).

notation.meaning: set on which convergence is uniform
parameter threshold independent of the point

source_refs.locator: G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175

source_witnesses.locator: G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175

children.title: Uniformity Domains
children.top_down_role: Domain choices governing where uniform approximation remains available.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniformity Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domains on which a smoothing family admits uniform error control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given functions \(f_\mu,f:D\to\mathbb R\), a nonempty subset \(U\subseteq D\) is a uniformity domain for \((f_\mu)_{\mu>0}\) relative to \(f\) if, with \[e_U(\mu):=\sup_{x\in U}|f_\mu(x)-f(x)|,\] one has \(e_U(\mu)<\infty\) for all sufficiently small \(\mu>0\) and \(e_U(\mu)\to0\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\). A class \(\mathcal U\subseteq\mathcal P(D)\setminus\{\varnothing\}\) specifies a uniformity regime when every \(U\in\mathcal U\) is a uniformity domain. When \(D\) is contained in a topological or normed space, common choices for \(\mathcal U\) include classes of compact or bounded subsets, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniformity domain is a nonempty set on which the worst smoothing error is finite for small parameters and tends to zero; a uniformity regime is a declared class of such domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U\) is a uniformity domain when \(e_U(\mu)<\infty\) eventually and \(e_U(\mu)\to0\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\).

notation.meaning: declared class of nonempty uniformity domains

source_refs.locator: G. Continuous and Uniform Convergence p. 175

children.title: Epi-Convergent Smoothing
children.top_down_role: Variational-limit behavior of smoothing families.

knowledge_statements.title: Epi-Convergent Smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential finite-dimensional definition of epi-convergence for smooth approximants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and let each \(f_\mu:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be smooth. The family is an epi-convergent smoothing of \(f\) if, for every sequence \(\mu_k\downarrow0\): (i) every \(x_k\to x\) satisfies \(\liminf_k f_{\mu_k}(x_k)\ge f(x)\); and (ii) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), some recovery sequence \(x_k\to x\) satisfies \(\limsup_k f_{\mu_k}(x_k)\le f(x)\). These two conditions are denoted by \(f_\mu\xrightarrow{e}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth approximants epi-converge when all convergent sequences satisfy the lower bound and every target point has a matching recovery sequence.
assumptions_latex: \(f_\mu:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is smooth for every \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_\mu\xrightarrow{e}f\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\).

source_refs.locator: B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

children.title: Minimizer Consistency
children.top_down_role: Transfer of minimizing behavior through the smoothing limit.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimizer Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cluster-point consistency for approximate global minimizers under epi-convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(f_k:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) epi-converges to a proper function \(f\). Let \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\) and choose \(x_k\) such that \[f_k(x_k)\le\inf f_k+\varepsilon_k.\] If a subsequence \((x_{k_j})\) converges to \(\bar x\), then \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\) and \[f_{k_j}(x_{k_j})\to\inf f.\] Thus epi-convergence makes every finite cluster point of asymptotically exact global minimizers consistent with the limiting problem, although it does not itself guarantee that such a cluster point exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite cluster point of increasingly accurate global minimizers of epi-convergent problems minimizes the limiting objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\) and \(f_{k_j}(x_{k_j})\to\inf f\).

notation.meaning: set of global minimizers of the limit objective

source_refs.locator: B. Epi-Convergence p. 240

children.title: Minimizer Recovery Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes supporting recovery of limiting minimizers from surrogate problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimizer Recovery Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global minimizer recovery under epi-convergence plus equi-coercivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let proper lower-semicontinuous functions \(f_k:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) epi-converge to a proper function \(f\), and assume equi-coercivity: for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), the union \(\bigcup_k\{x:f_k(x)\le\alpha\}\) is bounded. If \(\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\), then \[\inf f_k\to\inf f.\] Every sequence of \(\varepsilon_k\)-minimizers with \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\) is bounded and has cluster points in \(\operatorname*{argmin}f\). Conversely, each \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\) admits a recovery sequence \(x_k\to x^\star\) satisfying \(f_k(x_k)\to\inf f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equi-coercivity prevents escape, yielding convergence of optimal values, consistent cluster points, and recovery sequences for limiting minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf f_k\to\inf f\), and approximate minimizers recover \(\operatorname*{argmin}f\).

notation.meaning: global minimizer of the limit objective

children.title: Minimizer Escape Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Loss of minimizer consistency through noncompact or unstable surrogate behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimizer Escape Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of minimizer recovery without compactness or equi-coercivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mu>0\), define the smooth function \(f_\mu:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \[f_\mu(x)=(\mu x-1)^2.\] On every bounded set, \(f_\mu\to f\) uniformly as \(\mu\downarrow0\), where \(f(x)=1\); hence \(f_\mu\xrightarrow{e}f\). Nevertheless, \(\operatorname*{argmin}f_\mu=\{1/\mu\}\), so every selected minimizer escapes to infinity. Moreover, \(\inf f_\mu=0\) while \(\inf f=1\). Thus local uniform convergence and epi-convergence alone do not ensure minimizer or optimal-value recovery when approximate minimizers are not precompact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth minimizers can escape to infinity under epi-convergence, causing even optimal values to fail to converge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_\mu\xrightarrow{e}1\), but \(1/\mu\to\infty\) and \(\inf f_\mu\not\to\inf f\).

notation.meaning: unique minimizer of the smoothed objective

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Consistency Frameworks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke gradient consistency for smooth approximations of locally Lipschitz objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be locally Lipschitz and let \(f_\mu\) be continuously differentiable for every \(\mu>0\). The smoothing family is Clarke-gradient consistent at \(x\) if \[\operatorname*{Limsup}_{\substack{z\to x\\ \mu\downarrow0}}\{\nabla f_\mu(z)\}\subseteq\partial^C f(x).\] Equivalently, whenever \(z_k\to x\), \(\mu_k\downarrow0\), and \(\nabla f_{\mu_k}(z_k)\to v\), one has \(v\in\partial^C f(x)\). It is gradient consistent on \(D\) when this condition holds at every \(x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite limit of nearby smoothing gradients must belong to the Clarke subdifferential of the original objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{Limsup}_{z\to x,\,\mu\downarrow0}\{\nabla f_\mu(z)\}\subseteq\partial^C f(x)\).

notation.meaning: Clarke subdifferential of f at x
base point approaching x jointly with the parameter

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The outer-limit inclusion is a recognized Clarke-gradient consistency condition, but conventions differ across smoothing frameworks, including inclusion versus stronger equality formulations. An authoritative definition with a specific locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Max Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite maximum representation of a nonsmooth objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and open. A finite-max model on \(D\) is a function \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) represented by \[f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}\phi_i(x),\] where \(m\in\mathbb N\) and each \(\phi_i\in C^1(D)\). Its active index set at \(x\in D\) is \[I(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:\phi_i(x)=f(x)\}.\] The set \(I(x)\) is nonempty because the index set is finite. Nonsmoothness can occur at points where active components have different gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an open domain, a finite-max model is the maximum of finitely many continuously differentiable components, and its active indices are those attaining the maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}\phi_i(x)\) and \(I(x)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(x\in D\).

knowledge_statements.title: Compact Dual-Domain Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Max representation over a compact dual feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty and compact, let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, and let \(\psi:Q\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. A compact dual-domain max model has the representation \[f(x)=\max_{u\in Q}\{\langle Ax,u\rangle-\psi(u)\}.\] The maximum is attained for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). If \(Q\) is convex and \(\psi\) is convex, this is a convex max-structure suitable for dual smoothing by adding a strongly convex prox penalty in the maximization variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective is a maximum of affine-minus-continuous terms over a compact dual set, ensuring attainment for every primal point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\max_{u\in Q}\{\langle Ax,u\rangle-\psi(u)\}\), and the maximum is attained.

children.title: Separable Max Models
children.top_down_role: Max-structure models decomposed across independent components.

knowledge_statements.title: Separable Max Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additively separable max representation over disjoint primal blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in\mathbb N\), let \(n_j,m_j\in\mathbb N\), and write \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_p)\) with \(x_j\in\mathbb R^{n_j}\). For each \(j\), let \(Q_j\subseteq\mathbb R^{m_j}\) be nonempty and compact, let \(A_j:\mathbb R^{n_j}\to\mathbb R^{m_j}\) be linear, and let \(\psi_j:Q_j\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. A separable max model has the form \[f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^p\max_{u_j\in Q_j}\{\langle A_jx_j,u_j\rangle-\psi_j(u_j)\}.\] Equivalently, with \(Q=\prod_{j=1}^pQ_j\), evaluation of the maximum separates into \(p\) independent dual subproblems because the term indexed by \(j\) depends only on \((x_j,u_j)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable max model is a sum of compact-domain maximizations, each involving only one disjoint primal block and its corresponding dual variable.
assumptions_latex: \(\varnothing\neq Q_j\subseteq\mathbb R^{m_j}\) is compact for each \(j\).
\(A_j:\mathbb R^{n_j}\to\mathbb R^{m_j}\) is linear and \(\psi_j:Q_j\to\mathbb R\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^p\max_{u_j\in Q_j}\{\langle A_jx_j,u_j\rangle-\psi_j(u_j)\}\), with independent blockwise maximizations.

children.title: Block-Structured Max Models
children.top_down_role: Max-structure models organized through explicit variable or dual blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Structured Max Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sum of compact-domain max terms indexed by designated primal coordinate blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n,p\in\mathbb N\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). For each \(j=1,\ldots,p\), let \(B_j\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) be nonempty, let \(m_j\in\mathbb N\), let \(Q_j\subseteq\mathbb R^{m_j}\) be nonempty and compact, let \(A_j:\mathbb R^{|B_j|}\to\mathbb R^{m_j}\) be linear, and let \(\psi_j:Q_j\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. A block-structured max model is represented by \[f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^p\max_{u_j\in Q_j}\{\langle A_jx_{B_j},u_j\rangle-\psi_j(u_j)\}.\] Pairwise disjoint blocks give a separable model, while overlapping blocks introduce dependence between terms through their shared primal coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-structured max model sums compact-domain maximizations attached to specified coordinate blocks; overlapping blocks couple terms through shared coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(\varnothing\neq Q_j\subseteq\mathbb R^{m_j}\) is compact for each \(j\).
\(A_j:\mathbb R^{|B_j|}\to\mathbb R^{m_j}\) is linear and \(\psi_j:Q_j\to\mathbb R\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^p\max_{u_j\in Q_j}\{\langle A_jx_{B_j},u_j\rangle-\psi_j(u_j)\}\).

notation.meaning: coordinate index set of block j
subvector of x indexed by B_j
compact dual set for block j
number of coordinates in block B_j

children.title: Cross-Block Coupling
children.top_down_role: Structural interactions that limit blockwise decomposition.

assumptions_latex: Each \(Q_i\) is a nonempty compact convex set, \(A_i:X\to U_i^*\) is linear, and \(\phi:\prod_i Q_i\to\mathbb R\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is cross-block coupled precisely when no functions \(\phi_i:Q_i\to\mathbb R\) and constant \(c\) satisfy \(\phi(u_1,\ldots,u_m)=c+\sum_{i=1}^m\phi_i(u_i)\) on \(\prod_iQ_i\). In that case, evaluating \(F(x)\) generally requires the joint problem over \(\prod_iQ_i\), rather than \(m\) independent block maximizations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines coupling through failure of additive dual-block decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in X\), define \[F(x)=\max_{(u_1,\ldots,u_m)\in\prod_{i=1}^mQ_i}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\langle A_ix,u_i\rangle-\phi(u_1,\ldots,u_m)\right\}.\] The max representation has cross-block coupling when \(\phi\) is not additively separable on its product domain, meaning that there do not exist functions \(\phi_i:Q_i\to\mathbb R\) and \(c\in\mathbb R\) such that \(\phi(u_1,\ldots,u_m)=c+\sum_i\phi_i(u_i)\). Consequently, the maximizing blocks cannot in general be computed by independent blockwise maximizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block max model is cross-block coupled when its joint dual term is not a sum of independent block terms, so its maximizer generally requires joint computation.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Block Coupling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and matches the leaf, but the exact characterization of “cross-block coupling” is terminology-dependent and has no cited source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Composite representation and proximal maps for two-dimensional TV denoising
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents quadratic two-dimensional TV denoising through a horizontal–vertical difference operator and gives the explicit proximal maps of the isotropic and anisotropic difference aggregators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb E=\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(\mathbb V=\mathbb R^{m\times(n-1)}\times\mathbb R^{(m-1)\times n}\), \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|x-d\|_F^2\), and \(\mathcal A x=(p^x,q^x)\), where
\[
p^x_{i,j}=x_{i,j}-x_{i,j+1},\qquad q^x_{i,j}=x_{i,j}-x_{i+1,j}.
\]
Then quadratic TV denoising has the composite form \(\min_x\{f(x)+\lambda g(\mathcal A x)\}\), with
\[
g_I(p,q)=\sum_{i<m,j<n}\sqrt{p_{i,j}^2+q_{i,j}^2}+\sum_{j<n}|p_{m,j}|+\sum_{i<m}|q_{i,n}|
\]
in the isotropic case and
\[
g_{\ell_1}(p,q)=\sum_{i\le m,j<n}|p_{i,j}|+\sum_{i<m,j\le n}|q_{i,j}|
\]
in the anisotropic case. For \(\lambda>0\), write \(\mathcal T_\lambda(s)=\operatorname{sign}(s)\max\{|s|-\lambda,0\}\) and
\[
S_\lambda(a,b)=\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{\max\{\sqrt{a^2+b^2},\lambda\}}\right)(a,b).
\]
For \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g_I}(p,q)=(\tilde p,\tilde q)\), one has \((\tilde p_{i,j},\tilde q_{i,j})=S_\lambda(p_{i,j},q_{i,j})\) for \(i<m,j<n\), \(\tilde p_{m,j}=\mathcal T_\lambda(p_{m,j})\) for \(j<n\), and \(\tilde q_{i,n}=\mathcal T_\lambda(q_{i,n})\) for \(i<m\). For \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g_{\ell_1}}(p,q)=(\tilde p,\tilde q)\), every component satisfies \(\tilde p_{i,j}=\mathcal T_\lambda(p_{i,j})\) and \(\tilde q_{i,j}=\mathcal T_\lambda(q_{i,j})\) over its respective index range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The TV-denoising objective is a quadratic data-fit term plus a scaled function of the horizontal and vertical forward differences. The isotropic difference aggregator applies Euclidean norms to paired interior differences and absolute values to unmatched boundary differences, so its proximal map uses block Euclidean shrinkage in the interior and scalar soft-thresholding on the boundaries. The anisotropic aggregator is an entrywise absolute-value sum, so its proximal map soft-thresholds every difference component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_x\left\{\tfrac12\|x-d\|_F^2+\lambda\operatorname{TV}(x)\right\}=\min_x\{f(x)+\lambda g(\mathcal A x)\},\quad \operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g_I}\text{ is block shrinkage with scalar boundary shrinkage, and }\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g_{\ell_1}}\text{ is componentwise soft-thresholding.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean smoothing with a compact dual domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\max_{u\in Q}\{\langle Ax,u\rangle-\phi(u)\}\) and \[f_\mu(x)=\max_{u\in Q}\left\{\langle Ax,u\rangle-\phi(u)-\frac{\mu}{2}\|u-u_0\|_2^2\right\}.\] The regularized maximization has a unique solution \(u_\mu(x)\). Moreover, \(f_\mu\) is continuously differentiable with \(\nabla f_\mu(x)=A^*u_\mu(x)\), and its gradient is Lipschitz with constant at most \(\|A\|_{2\to2}^2/\mu\). If \(D=\max_{u\in Q}\tfrac12\|u-u_0\|_2^2\), then \(0\le f(x)-f_\mu(x)\le\mu D\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic dual regularization gives a unique dual maximizer, a smooth primal surrogate, gradient Lipschitz constant at most squared operator norm divided by the smoothing parameter, and controlled bias.

children.title: Entropic Dual-Prox Geometry
children.top_down_role: Entropy-based geometry used for dual smoothing.

knowledge_statements.title: Entropic Dual-Prox Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-entropy prox geometry on a finite probability simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q\in\mathbb R_{++}^m\) satisfy \(\sum_{i=1}^m q_i=1\), and let \(\Delta_m=\{u\in\mathbb R_+^m:\sum_{i=1}^m u_i=1\}\). Define \[d(u)=\sum_{i=1}^m u_i\log\!\left(\frac{u_i}{q_i}\right),\qquad 0\log 0:=0.\] For \(u\in\operatorname{ri}\Delta_m\) and \(v\in\Delta_m\), the associated Bregman divergence is \[D_d(v,u)=d(v)-d(u)-\langle\nabla d(u),v-u\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^m v_i\log\!\left(\frac{v_i}{u_i}\right).\] It satisfies \[D_d(v,u)\ge \frac12\|v-u\|_1^2.\] Thus \(d\) is \(1\)-strongly convex relative to \(\|\cdot\|_1\) under the convention \(D_d(v,u)\ge\tfrac12\|v-u\|_1^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative entropy generates Kullback–Leibler Bregman divergence on the simplex, which dominates one half of the squared l1 distance and gives unit strong convexity in the l1 geometry.
assumptions_latex: \(q\in\mathbb R_{++}^m\) satisfies \(\sum_{i=1}^m q_i=1\), and \(\Delta_m=\{u\in\mathbb R_+^m:\sum_{i=1}^m u_i=1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(u\in\operatorname{ri}\Delta_m\) and \(v\in\Delta_m\), \(D_d(v,u)=\sum_i v_i\log(v_i/u_i)\ge\tfrac12\|v-u\|_1^2\), so \(d\) has strong-convexity modulus \(1\) relative to \(\|\cdot\|_1\).

notation.meaning: Relative-entropy prox centered at the positive reference distribution.
Bregman divergence generated by the entropy prox.

children.title: Simplex-Constrained Dual Domains
children.top_down_role: Dual smoothing over simplex-structured feasible regions.

assumptions_latex: The dual variable has \(m\ge2\) nonnegative coordinates representing mixture weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A dual feasible set is simplex-constrained when it equals \(\Delta_m\), or a nonempty closed convex subset thereof, so every feasible dual vector is a probability distribution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional probability-simplex dual domains.

source_refs.locator: A. Convex Sets and Functions p. 38

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The standard simplex-constrained dual domain is \[\Delta_m=\left\{u\in\mathbb R^m: u_i\ge0\ \text{for every }i,\ \sum_{i=1}^m u_i=1\right\}.\] More generally, a dual domain \(Q\) is simplex-constrained when \(Q\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of \(\Delta_m\). Thus every \(u\in Q\) is a probability vector, and linear dual pairings take the form \(\langle z,u\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^m z_i u_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplex-constrained dual variable is a probability vector: its coordinates are nonnegative and sum to one, possibly with additional closed convex restrictions.
knowledge_statements.title: Simplex-Constrained Dual Domains

children.title: Boundary-Sensitive Entropic Regimes
children.top_down_role: Behavior associated with simplex faces or vanishing dual coordinates.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(d\) is finite on the boundary, \((\nabla d(u))_i=1+\log(u_i/q_i)\to-\infty\) as \(u_i\downarrow0\); moreover, \(D_d(v,u)=+\infty\) whenever \(u_i=0<v_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the boundary singularity of simplex entropy geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The entropy prox \(d\) extends continuously and finitely to \(\Delta_m\), but its gradient exists only on \(\operatorname{ri}\Delta_m\), with \[(\nabla d(u))_i=1+\log\!\left(\frac{u_i}{q_i}\right).\] Hence \((\nabla d(u))_i\to-\infty\) when \(u_i\downarrow0\). Under the extended-value convention for relative entropy, \[D_d(v,u)=\sum_i v_i\log\!\left(\frac{v_i}{u_i}\right)=+\infty\] whenever some coordinate satisfies \(u_i=0<v_i\). Therefore mirror or smoothing formulas requiring a finite gradient at the reference point must keep that point in \(\operatorname{ri}\Delta_m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Entropy remains finite at simplex boundary points, but its gradient becomes singular; relative entropy is infinite when positive mass moves into a zero reference coordinate.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Sensitive Entropic Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary behavior and failure-boundary content kind are mathematically appropriate, but the entropy-gradient singularity and extended relative-entropy claim have no cited source.

knowledge_statements.title: Problem-Adapted Dual-Prox Smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional norm-adapted dual smoothing for compact max representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(U\) be finite-dimensional real normed spaces, let \(Q\subset U\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(A:X	o U^*\) be linear. Suppose \(\phi:Q	o\mathbb R\) is convex and \(d:Q	o\mathbb R\) is continuous, satisfies \(\min_Q d=0\), and is \(\sigma\)-strongly convex relative to \(\|\cdot\|_U\), where \(\sigma>0\). For \(\mu>0\), define \[f(x)=\max_{u\in Q}\{\langle Ax,uangle-\phi(u)\},\qquad f_\mu(x)=\max_{u\in Q}\{\langle Ax,uangle-\phi(u)-\mu d(u)\}.\] The maximizer \(u_\mu(x)\) is unique, \(f_\mu\) is continuously differentiable, and \[
abla f_\mu(x)=A^*u_\mu(x).\] With the dual norm on \(X^*\), \[\|
abla f_\mu(x)-
abla f_\mu(y)\|_{X^*}\le rac{\|A\|_{X	o U^*}^2}{\mu\sigma}\|x-y\|_X.\] If \(D=\max_{u\in Q}d(u)\), then \[0\le f(x)-f_\mu(x)\le\mu D\qquad	ext{for every }x\in X.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly convex dual prox geometry adapted to the feasible set gives a unique dual response, a smooth surrogate with a norm-dependent gradient Lipschitz bound, and bias controlled by the prox diameter.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(U\) are finite-dimensional real normed spaces, \(Q\subset U\) is nonempty, compact, and convex, and \(A:X\to U^*\) is linear.
\(\phi:Q\to\mathbb R\) is convex, and \(d:Q\to\mathbb R\) is continuous, satisfies \(\min_Qd=0\), and is \(\sigma\)-strongly convex relative to \(\|\cdot\|_U\), with \(\sigma>0\) and \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
The maximizer \(u_\mu(x)\) is unique, \(
abla f_\mu(x)=A^*u_\mu(x)\), \(\|
abla f_\mu(x)-
abla f_\mu(y)\|_{X^*}\le\|A\|_{X	o U^*}^2\|x-y\|_X/(\mu\sigma)\), and \(0\le f(x)-f_\mu(x)\le\mu\max_Qd\).

notation.meaning: Strong-convexity modulus of the prox geometry.
Maximum prox value controlling smoothing bias.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Support Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugate representation of prox-regularized support functions in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, let \(Q\subset U\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(d:Q\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and strongly convex. For \(\mu>0\), define the extended-value function \[g_\mu(u)=\begin{cases}\mu d(u),&u\in Q,\\+\infty,&u\notin Q.\end{cases}\] For \(z\in U\), the prox-regularized support function has the representation \[\sigma_{Q,\mu}(z)=\max_{u\in Q}\{\langle z,u\rangle-\mu d(u)\}=g_\mu^*(z).\] Its maximizing point \(u_\mu(z)\) is unique, and \[\nabla\sigma_{Q,\mu}(z)=u_\mu(z).\] If \(\min_Qd=0\) and \(D=\max_{u\in Q}d(u)\), then \[0\le\sigma_Q(z)-\sigma_{Q,\mu}(z)\le\mu D.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A prox-regularized support function is the conjugate of the extended-value prox regularizer on the set; it is differentiable, with gradient equal to its unique regularized support maximizer.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, \(Q\subset U\) is nonempty, compact, and convex, and \(d:Q\to\mathbb R\) is continuous and strongly convex.
\(g_\mu(u)=\mu d(u)\) for \(u\in Q\) and \(g_\mu(u)=+\infty\) otherwise, with \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The identity \(\sigma_{Q,\mu}=g_\mu^*\) holds, the maximizing point \(u_\mu(z)\) is unique, and \(\nabla\sigma_{Q,\mu}(z)=u_\mu(z)\); if \(\min_Qd=0\), then \(0\le\sigma_Q(z)-\sigma_{Q,\mu}(z)\le\mu\max_Qd\).

notation.meaning: Convex conjugate of the extended-value prox regularizer.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) and \(U\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(X\subset E\) be open and convex, and let \(Q\subset U\) be nonempty, compact, and convex. Suppose \(\Phi:X	imes Q	o\mathbb R\) is continuous, convex in \(x\), concave in \(u\), continuously differentiable in \(x\), and has jointly continuous partial gradient \(
abla_x\Phi\). Let \(d:Q	o\mathbb R\) be continuous and strongly convex. For \(\mu>0\), define \[V_\mu(x)=\max_{u\in Q}\{\Phi(x,u)-\mu d(u)\}.\] For every \(x\in X\), the maximizer \(u_\mu(x)\) is unique. The function \(V_\mu\) is convex and continuously differentiable on \(X\), with \[
abla V_\mu(x)=
abla_x\Phi(x,u_\mu(x)).\]

Under the exact first-order oracle model, its iterates satisfy \[F_\mu(x_k)-F_\mu(x_\mu^*)\le\frac{2L_\mu\|x_0-x_\mu^*\|^2}{(k+1)^2}=\frac{2L_\mu R^2}{(k+1)^2}.\] Therefore, to obtain \(F_\mu(x_k)-F_\mu(x_\mu^*)\le\delta\), it suffices that \[k+1\ge\sqrt{\frac{2L_\mu R^2}{\delta}}.\] The bound concerns optimization of the fixed surrogate and does not include its approximation bias relative to the original nonsmooth objective.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: An objective-accuracy guarantee obtained by coupling the smoothing parameter to the requested tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(H=f+h+g\) satisfies Assumptions (A)--(E): \(f\) is \(L_f\)-smooth with \(L_f\ge0\); \(h\) is \((\alpha,\beta)\)-smoothable with \(\alpha,beta>0\) and the stated \(1/\mu\)-smooth approximations; \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex; the specified level sets are bounded; and \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}H\ne\varnothing\). Fix \(\bar\varepsilon>0\) and \(\varepsilon\in(0,\bar\varepsilon)\), and let \(\{x^k\}_{k\ge0}\) be generated by S-FISTA with \[\mu=\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{\alpha\beta}+\sqrt{\alpha\beta+L_f\varepsilon}}}.\] Define \[\Gamma=\left(R_{H(x^0)+\varepsilon/2}+\|x^0\|\right)^2.\] Then every integer \(k\) satisfying \[k\ge 2\sqrt{2\alpha\beta\Gamma}\,\varepsilon^{-1}+\sqrt{2L_f\Gamma}\,\varepsilon^{-1/2}\] obeys \(H(x^k)-H_{\mathrm{opt}}\le\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Valued Convex Envelopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space convex Moreau envelope with positive parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:H	o(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(\lambda>0\). For \(x\in H\), define \[e_\lambda f(x)=\inf_{y\in H}\left\{f(y)+ rac{1}{2\lambda}\|x-y\|^2ight\}.\] The envelope \(e_\lambda f\) is finite and convex on \(H\), and the infimum is attained at the unique point \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\). Moreover, \(e_\lambda f\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable and \[
abla e_\lambda f(x)= rac{x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)}{\lambda}.\] For all \(x,z\in H\), \[\|
abla e_\lambda f(x)-
abla e_\lambda f(z)\|\le rac1\lambda\|x-z\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a real Hilbert space, the Moreau envelope is finite and convex everywhere, has a unique proximal minimizer, and is continuously differentiable with a gradient Lipschitz constant at most one over the parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The envelope \(e_\lambda f\) is finite and convex on \(H\), its defining infimum has the unique minimizer \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\), and \(\nabla e_\lambda f(x)=\lambda^{-1}(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x))\) is \(1/\lambda\)-Lipschitz.

notation.meaning: Unique proximal point of f at x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moreau Envelope of a Convex-Set Indicator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection and squared-distance representation of the envelope of an indicator function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(\mu>0\), and set \(f=\delta_C\). Then, for every \(x\in\mathbb E\),
\[
M_f^\mu(x)=\delta_C(P_C(x))+ rac{1}{2\mu}\|x-P_C(x)\|^2
= rac{1}{2\mu}d_C(x)^2,
\]
where \(d_C(x):=\inf_{y\in C}\|x-y\|\). Hence
\[
M_{\delta_C}^\mu=\frac{1}{2\mu}d_C^2.
\]

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is prox-bounded exactly when \(\lambda_f>0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional definition using nondegeneracy of the quadratic infimal convolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is prox-bounded if there exist \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\lambda>0\) such that \[e_\lambda f(x):=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\right\}>-\infty.\] Its threshold of prox-boundedness is \[\lambda_f:=\sup\left\{\lambda>0:\text{there exists }x\in\mathbb{R}^n\text{ with }e_\lambda f(x)>-\infty\right\}.\] Accordingly, prox-boundedness means \(\lambda_f>0\); parameters strictly below \(\lambda_f\) lie in the proper-envelope regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is prox-bounded when some quadratic regularization has a finite infimum; the supremum of admissible parameters is its prox-boundedness threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Bounded Envelopes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and threshold convention are standard and fit the leaf, but they lack a citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(0)=\{-\lambda,\lambda\}\), so the proximal mapping is multivalued and \(e_\lambda f\) is not differentiable at \(0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit prox-bounded nonconvex example exhibiting branching and envelope nonsmoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(y)=-|y|\) is proper, continuous, and prox-bounded, but it is not weakly convex for any finite modulus. Direct minimization gives \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)=\begin{cases}\{x+\lambda\},&x>0,\\ \{-\lambda,\lambda\},&x=0,\\ \{x-\lambda\},&x<0,\end{cases}\qquad e_\lambda f(x)=-|x|-\frac{\lambda}{2}.\] Hence the proximal mapping branches at \(x=0\), and the associated Moreau envelope fails to be differentiable there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The prox-bounded function minus absolute value has two proximal points at zero, and its Moreau envelope retains a cusp there.

knowledge_statements.title: Envelope Differentiability Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient smooth regime and sharp loss of uniqueness at the curvature threshold for a positive weak-convexity modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\rho>0\). For \(0<\lambda<\rho^{-1}\), the proximal objective is strongly convex, so \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}\) is single-valued and \(e_\lambda f\) is continuously differentiable. This strict inequality is essential in general. For \(f(y)=-(\rho/2)y^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) and \(\lambda=\rho^{-1}\), the proximal objective at \(x=0\) is identically zero, so every \(y\in\mathbb{R}\) is proximal. For \(\lambda>\rho^{-1}\), its infimum is \(-\infty\). Thus smoothness and even properness can fail at and beyond the threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive weak-convexity modulus, the envelope is smooth strictly below the reciprocal curvature threshold; at the threshold proximal uniqueness can fail, and beyond it the envelope can collapse.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_\lambda f\in C^1(\mathbb{R}^n)\); at or beyond the threshold, differentiability is not guaranteed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smoothness and gradient of the Huber function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The Huber function is the Moreau smoothing of the norm; the statement includes both branches and their common boundary convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $\mu>0$ and define
\[
H_\mu(x)=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{2\mu}\lVert x\rVert^2,&\lVert x\rVert\leq\mu,\\
\lVert x\rVert-\dfrac{\mu}{2},&\lVert x\rVert>\mu.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $H_\mu$ is $1/\mu$-smooth and, with $f(x)=\lVert x\rVert$,
\[
\nabla H_\mu(x)=\frac1\mu\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\mu f}(x)\bigr)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{x}{\mu},&\lVert x\rVert\leq\mu,\\
\dfrac{x}{\lVert x\rVert},&\lVert x\rVert>\mu.
\end{cases}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For positive μ, the Huber function is 1/μ-smooth. Its gradient is the scaled proximal residual for the norm: x/μ when the norm of x is at most μ, and x divided by its norm when the norm exceeds μ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H_\mu\text{ is }\mu^{-1}\text{-smooth and }\nabla H_\mu(x)=\mu^{-1}(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\mu f}(x))=\begin{cases}x/\mu,&\lVert x\rVert\leq\mu,\\x/\lVert x\rVert,&\lVert x\rVert>\mu.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The proximal optimality condition and envelope-gradient formula give \[
abla e_\lambda f(x)= rac{x-p}{\lambda}\in\partial f(p).\] Consequently, \[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(p))\leq\lVert
abla e_\lambda f(x)Vert,\qquad \lVert x-pVert=\lambda\lVert
abla e_\lambda f(x)Vert.\] Moreover, \(
abla e_\lambda f(x)=0\) holds if and only if \(p=x\), which is equivalent to \(0\in\partial f(x)\). Thus the envelope gradient simultaneously measures displacement to a nearby point and certifies its subgradient residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The envelope gradient is a subgradient at the proximal point, controls its stationarity residual, and vanishes exactly at stationary points.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the Pasch-Hausdorff envelope by \[f_k(x):=\inf_{y\in X}\left\{f(y)+k d(x,y)\right\}.\] Then \(f_k\) is finite-valued, \(k\)-Lipschitz, and satisfies \(f_k\leq f\). knowledge_statements.title: Huber-Type Smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar Huber smoothing of the absolute-value kink, with transition half-width \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\mu>0\), the Huber-type smoothing of \(|t|\) is the continuously differentiable convex function
\[
h_\mu(t)=\begin{cases}t^2/(2\mu),&|t|\leq\mu,\\ |t|-\mu/2,&|t|>\mu.\end{cases}
\]
Its derivative is \(h_\mu'(t)=t/\mu\) when \(|t|\leq\mu\) and \(h_\mu'(t)=\operatorname{sign}(t)\) otherwise. Moreover, \(0\leq |t|-h_\mu(t)\leq\mu/2\) for every \(t\in\mathbb R\), and \(h_\mu(t)\to |t|\) uniformly as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Huber smoothing replaces the absolute-value kink by a quadratic segment, retains linear tails, and approximates absolute value uniformly within μ/2.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_\mu\in C^1(\mathbb R)\) is convex and \(0\leq |t|-h_\mu(t)\leq\mu/2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Huber Smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Analytic square-root smoothing normalized to converge to \(|t|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\mu>0\), define the pseudo-Huber smoothing by
\[
p_\mu(t)=\mu\!\left(\sqrt{1+(t/\mu)^2}-1\right)=\sqrt{t^2+\mu^2}-\mu.
\]
Then \(p_\mu\) is convex and real analytic, with \(p_\mu'(t)=t/\sqrt{t^2+\mu^2}\) and \(p_\mu''(t)=\mu^2/(t^2+\mu^2)^{3/2}>0\). For every \(t\in\mathbb R\), \(0\leq |t|-p_\mu(t)\leq\mu\); hence \(p_\mu\to |\cdot|\) uniformly as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pseudo-Huber smoothing is an analytic convex square-root approximation to absolute value whose uniform error is at most μ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_\mu\) is analytic and strictly convex, and \(0\leq |t|-p_\mu(t)\leq\mu\).

knowledge_statements.title: Log-Sum-Exp Smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth approximation of a pointwise maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R\), \(m\geq1\), and \(\mu>0\). The log-sum-exp smoothing of \(\max_i a_i\) is
\[
L_\mu(a)=\mu\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m e^{a_i/\mu}\right).
\]
It satisfies
\[
\max_i a_i\leq L_\mu(a)\leq\max_i a_i+\mu\log m,
\]
and \(\nabla_iL_\mu(a)=e^{a_i/\mu}/\sum_j e^{a_j/\mu}\). Thus \(L_\mu\) is convex and smooth and converges uniformly on \(\mathbb R^m\), in absolute error, to the maximum as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Log-sum-exp smoothly overestimates a finite maximum by at most μ log m, with gradient equal to the softmax weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_i a_i\leq L_\mu(a)\leq\max_i a_i+\mu\log m\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary finite log-sum-exp representation and sharp additive bound
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hessian bound for entropy smoothing of eigenvalues
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded differentiability and curvature guarantee for spectral log-sum-exp smoothing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb N\) and define \(E:\mathbb S_n\to\mathbb R\) by \(E(X)=\ln\sum_{i=1}^n e^{\lambda^{(i)}(X)}\). Then \(E\) is twice Fr\'echet differentiable on \(\mathbb S_n\), and for every \(X,H\in\mathbb S_n\), \[\langle\nabla^2E(X)H,H\rangle_F\le\|H\|_{(\infty)}^2,\] where \(\langle A,B\rangle_F=\operatorname{Tr}(AB)\) and \(\|H\|_{(\infty)}\) is the spectral norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The spectral log-sum-exp function is twice Fréchet differentiable on the symmetric matrices, and its Hessian quadratic form in every symmetric direction is at most the square of that direction's spectral norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E\in C^2(\mathbb S_n)\quad\text{and}\quad\langle\nabla^2E(X)H,H\rangle_F\le\|H\|_{(\infty)}^2\quad\forall X,H\in\mathbb S_n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient and Hessian representations for symmetric log-sum-exp smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First- and second-order differential formulas for the symmetric log-sum-exp smoothing of finitely many linear forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mu>0\), \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R^n\), and
\[
f_\mu(x)=\mu\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\left[e^{\langle a_i,x\rangle/\mu}+e^{-\langle a_i,x\rangle/\mu}\right]\right).
\]
Define
\[
\omega_\mu(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\left(e^{\langle a_i,x\rangle/\mu}+e^{-\langle a_i,x\rangle/\mu}\right),
\qquad
\lambda_\mu^{(i)}(x)=\frac{e^{\langle a_i,x\rangle/\mu}-e^{-\langle a_i,x\rangle/\mu}}{\omega_\mu(x)}.
\]
Then \(f_\mu\in C^2(\mathbb R^n)\), and for every \(x,h\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
\langle\nabla f_\mu(x),h\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_\mu^{(i)}(x)\langle a_i,h\rangle,
\]
\[
\langle\nabla^2f_\mu(x)h,h\rangle
=\frac1\mu\sum_{i=1}^m\frac{\langle a_i,h\rangle^2}{\omega_\mu(x)}\left(e^{\langle a_i,x\rangle/\mu}+e^{-\langle a_i,x\rangle/\mu}\right)
-\frac1\mu\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_\mu^{(i)}(x)\langle a_i,h\rangle\right)^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The symmetric log-sum-exp smoothing is twice continuously differentiable. Its directional gradient is a signed exponentially weighted combination of the linear forms, while its Hessian quadratic form is the corresponding weighted second moment minus the squared weighted first moment, divided by mu.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x,h\in\mathbb R^n:\quad f_\mu\in C^2(\mathbb R^n),\quad \langle\nabla f_\mu(x),h\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_\mu^{(i)}(x)\langle a_i,h\rangle,\quad \langle\nabla^2f_\mu(x)h,h\rangle=\frac1\mu\sum_{i=1}^m\frac{\langle a_i,h\rangle^2\left(e^{\langle a_i,x\rangle/\mu}+e^{-\langle a_i,x\rangle/\mu}\right)}{\omega_\mu(x)}-\frac1\mu\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_\mu^{(i)}(x)\langle a_i,h\rangle\right)^2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-Shift Evaluation of Scaled Log-Sum-Exp
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact maximum-shift procedure for evaluating scaled log-sum-exp with nonpositive shifted exponential arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(\mu>0\) and \(u\in\mathbb{R}^m\), compute
\[
\bar u=\max_{1\le j\le m}u^{(j)},\qquad v^{(j)}=u^{(j)}-\bar u\quad(j=1,\ldots,m).
\]
Then compute
\[
\eta(v)=\mu\log\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^m e^{v^{(j)}/\mu}\right)
\]
and output
\[
\eta(u)=\bar u+\eta(v).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtract the largest component of u, evaluate scaled log-sum-exp at the shifted vector, and add the largest component back.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \eta(u)=\bar u+\eta(v),\qquad \bar u=\max_j u^{(j)},\quad v=u-\bar u\mathbf 1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-Shift Equivariance and Gradient Invariance of Log-Sum-Exp
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact translation identities underlying stable evaluation of scaled log-sum-exp and its gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mu>0\) and define
\[
\eta(z)=\mu\log\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^m e^{z^{(j)}/\mu}\right).
\]
For \(u\in\mathbb{R}^m\), set
\[
\bar u=\max_{1\le j\le m}u^{(j)},\qquad v^{(j)}=u^{(j)}-\bar u.
\]
Then
\[
\eta(u)=\bar u+\eta(v),\qquad \nabla\eta(u)=\nabla\eta(v).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After subtracting the maximum component from every component of u, the log-sum-exp value decreases by that maximum while its gradient remains unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \eta(u)=\bar u+\eta(v)\quad\text{and}\quad\nabla\eta(u)=\nabla\eta(v)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stable Maximum-Shift Principle for Log-Sum-Exp
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the exact shift identities with the sign structure used for stable evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mu>0\), \(u\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and
\[
\eta(z)=\mu\log\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^m e^{z^{(j)}/\mu}\right).
\]
Set
\[
\bar u=\max_j u^{(j)},\qquad v^{(j)}=u^{(j)}-\bar u.
\]
Then
\[
v^{(j)}\le 0\quad(j=1,\ldots,m),\qquad \max_j v^{(j)}=0,
\]
and
\[
\eta(u)=\bar u+\eta(v),\qquad \nabla\eta(u)=\nabla\eta(v).
\]
Thus the value and gradient can be evaluated from shifted exponential arguments that are all nonpositive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting the largest component makes every shifted component nonpositive and at least one equal to zero. Adding the maximum back recovers the original value, while the gradient is unchanged, so the exponential arguments used in the shifted evaluation are never positive.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximation bounds and gradient of spectral log-sum-exp smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives both the uniform maximal-eigenvalue approximation gap and the exact gradient of the spectral log-sum-exp smoothing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(\mu>0\), and \(f_\mu(X)=\mu\ln(\operatorname{Tr}(e^{X/\mu}))\) for \(X\in S_n\). Then every \(X\in S_n\) satisfies \[\lambda_{\max}(X)\le f_\mu(X)\le\lambda_{\max}(X)+\mu\ln n.\] Moreover, \(f_\mu\) is differentiable on \(S_n\). For a spectral decomposition \(X=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda^{(i)}(X)u_i(X)u_i(X)^T\) with unit eigenvectors, \[\nabla f_\mu(X)=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n e^{\lambda^{(i)}(X)/\mu}u_i(X)u_i(X)^T}{\sum_{i=1}^n e^{\lambda^{(i)}(X)/\mu}}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient Lipschitz bound for symmetric log-sum-exp smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smoothing-specific Hessian and gradient bound in a primal-dual ellipsoidal norm pair, derived from uniform bounds on the generating vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(G\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be positive definite, and define \(\|h\|_G=\sqrt{\langle Gh,h\rangle}\) and \(\|s\|_G^*=\sqrt{\langle G^{-1}s,s\rangle}\). Assume
\[
\|a_i\|_G^*\le\nu\sqrt n\qquad(i=1,\ldots,m).
\]
For \(\mu>0\), define
\[
f_\mu(x)=\mu\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\left[e^{\langle a_i,x\rangle/\mu}+e^{-\langle a_i,x\rangle/\mu}\right]\right).
\]
Then \(f_\mu\in C^2(\mathbb R^n)\), and for every \(x,h\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
\langle\nabla^2f_\mu(x)h,h\rangle\le\frac{\nu^2n}{\mu}\|h\|_G^2.
\]
In particular, for every \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
\|\nabla f_\mu(x)-\nabla f_\mu(y)\|_G^*\le\frac{\nu^2n}{\mu}\|x-y\|_G.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If each generating vector has dual G-norm at most nu times the square root of n, then the symmetric log-sum-exp smoothing has Hessian bounded above by nu squared times n divided by mu in the G-norm. Its gradient is consequently Lipschitz in the associated primal-dual norm pair with the same constant.

knowledge_statements.title: Softplus Smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logistic smoothing of the positive-part function \((t)_+\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\mu>0\), the softplus smoothing of \((t)_+=\max\{0,t\}\) is
\[
s_\mu(t)=\mu\log\!\left(1+e^{t/\mu}\right).
\]
It is convex and infinitely differentiable, with \(s_\mu'(t)=(1+e^{-t/\mu})^{-1}\) and \(s_\mu''(t)=e^{-t/\mu}/\bigl(\mu(1+e^{-t/\mu})^2\bigr)>0\). For every \(t\in\mathbb R\),
\[
(t)_+\leq s_\mu(t)\leq(t)_++\mu\log2,
\]
so \(s_\mu\to(\cdot)_+\) uniformly as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Softplus is a smooth convex approximation of the positive part, overestimating it by no more than μ log 2.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((t)_+\leq s_\mu(t)\leq(t)_++\mu\log2\).

notation.meaning: positive part, equal to the maximum of zero and t

knowledge_statements.title: Soft-Min Smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth underapproximation of a pointwise minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R\), \(m\geq1\), and \(\mu>0\). Define the soft minimum by
\[
M_\mu(a)=-\mu\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m e^{-a_i/\mu}\right).
\]
Equivalently, \(M_\mu(a)=-L_\mu(-a)\). It is smooth and concave, with \(\nabla_iM_\mu(a)=e^{-a_i/\mu}/\sum_j e^{-a_j/\mu}\), and satisfies
\[
\min_i a_i-\mu\log m\leq M_\mu(a)\leq\min_i a_i.
\]
Consequently it converges uniformly, in absolute error, to the minimum as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Soft-min smoothly underestimates a finite minimum by at most μ log m and is the negative log-sum-exp of negated inputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_i a_i-\mu\log m\leq M_\mu(a)\leq\min_i a_i\).

knowledge_statements.title: Absolute-Value Smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Square-root smoothing of \(|t|\), without subtractive normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\mu>0\), define
\[
a_\mu(t)=\sqrt{t^2+\mu^2}.
\]
Then \(a_\mu\) is an even, convex, real-analytic smoothing of \(|t|\), with \(a_\mu'(t)=t/\sqrt{t^2+\mu^2}\) and \(a_\mu''(t)=\mu^2/(t^2+\mu^2)^{3/2}>0\). For all \(t\in\mathbb R\),
\[
|t|\leq a_\mu(t)\leq |t|+\mu.
\]
Therefore \(a_\mu\to|\cdot|\) uniformly as \(\mu\downarrow0\), while the kink is replaced by a transition region of scale \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The square-root model smoothly overestimates absolute value by at most μ and replaces its kink with an analytic transition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_\mu\) is analytic and strictly convex, with \(|t|\leq a_\mu(t)\leq|t|+\mu\).

knowledge_statements.title: Hinge Smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-linear smoothing of the scalar hinge \((t)_+\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\mu>0\), define the smoothed hinge
\[
q_\mu(t)=\begin{cases}0,&t\leq0,\\ t^2/(2\mu),&0<t<\mu,\\ t-\mu/2,&t\geq\mu.\end{cases}
\]
Then \(q_\mu\) is convex and continuously differentiable, with derivative \(0\) on \(( -\infty,0]\), \(t/\mu\) on \((0,\mu)\), and \(1\) on \([\mu,\infty)\). For every \(t\in\mathbb R\),
\[
0\leq(t)_+-q_\mu(t)\leq\mu/2,
\]
so \(q_\mu\to(\cdot)_+\) uniformly as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic hinge smoothing joins the zero and linear regimes across an interval of width μ, with uniform error at most μ/2.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_\mu\in C^1(\mathbb R)\) is convex and \(0\leq(t)_+-q_\mu(t)\leq\mu/2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Shared Kink-Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer identity between absolute-value and hinge smoothings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(a_\mu:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be an even continuously differentiable approximation of \(|\cdot|\), and define
\[
r_\mu(t)=\frac{t+a_\mu(t)}{2}.
\]
Then \(r_\mu\) approximates \((t)_+\) because \((t)_+=(t+|t|)/2\), and
\[
\left|r_\mu(t)-(t)_+\right|=\frac12\left|a_\mu(t)-|t|\right|.
\]
Moreover, \(r_\mu'(t)=(1+a_\mu'(t))/2\). Hence any transition of \(a_\mu'\) from \(-1\) to \(1\) induces, on the same scale, a hinge-gradient transition from \(0\) to \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An absolute-value smoothing induces a hinge smoothing by halving its sum with t; approximation error is halved and the transition scale is preserved.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_\mu=(\operatorname{id}+a_\mu)/2\) and \(|r_\mu-(\cdot)_+|=|a_\mu-|\cdot||/2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise Linear-Quadratic Smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moreau-envelope construction for convex piecewise-linear objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and piecewise linear. For \(\mu>0\), its quadratic Moreau smoothing is
\[
f_\mu(x)=\min_{y\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\mu}\|x-y\|^2\right\}.
\]
The minimizer \(y=\operatorname{prox}_{\mu f}(x)\) is unique, \(f_\mu\) is convex and continuously differentiable, and
\[
\nabla f_\mu(x)=\mu^{-1}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\mu f}(x)\bigr).
\]
Furthermore, \(f_\mu\) is piecewise linear-quadratic and increases pointwise to \(f\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic infimal convolution turns a proper closed convex piecewise-linear function into a differentiable convex piecewise linear-quadratic function.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and piecewise linear
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_\mu\in C^1(\mathbb R^n)\) is convex and piecewise linear-quadratic, with \(f_\mu(x)\uparrow f(x)\).

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of f with parameter μ

knowledge_statements.title: Mollifier Smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convolution smoothing by a normalized smooth mollifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)\), and let \(\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)\) satisfy \(\rho\geq0\) and \(\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho(u)\,du=1\). For \(\mu>0\), set \(\rho_\mu(u)=\mu^{-n}\rho(u/\mu)\) and
\[
f_\mu(x)=(f*\rho_\mu)(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x-u)\rho_\mu(u)\,du.
\]
Then \(f_\mu\in C^\infty\), and \(f_\mu\to f\) in \(L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\). At every continuity point of \(f\), convergence also holds pointwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convolution with a rescaled smooth probability kernel produces an infinitely differentiable approximation converging locally in integral and at continuity points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f*\rho_\mu\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n)\) and \(f*\rho_\mu\to f\) in \(L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Gaussian Smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convolution and expectation forms of isotropic Gaussian smoothing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be measurable and satisfy \(\mathbb E|f(x+\mu Z)|<\infty\) for every \(x\), where \(Z\sim N(0,I_n)\) and \(\mu>0\). Gaussian smoothing is
\[
f_\mu(x)=\mathbb E[f(x+\mu Z)]=(2\pi\mu^2)^{-n/2}\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y)e^{-\|x-y\|^2/(2\mu^2)}\,dy.
\]
Whenever differentiation under the expectation is justified, it satisfies
\[
\nabla f_\mu(x)=\mu^{-1}\mathbb E[f(x+\mu Z)Z].
\]
If \(f\) is continuous with suitable growth, then \(f_\mu(x)\to f(x)\) as \(\mu\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian smoothing equals averaging over isotropic Gaussian perturbations and admits a zeroth-order expectation formula for its gradient.

differentiation under the expectation is justified

knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Kernel Smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Localized convolution smoothing using a compactly supported probability kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)\) satisfy \(K\geq0\), \(\int_{\mathbb R^n}K(u)\,du=1\), and \(\operatorname{supp}K\subseteq\{u:\|u\|\leq1\}\). For \(\mu>0\), define \(K_\mu(u)=\mu^{-n}K(u/\mu)\) and
\[
f_\mu(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x-u)K_\mu(u)\,du.
\]
Thus \(f_\mu(x)\) depends only on values of \(f\) in the closed ball of radius \(\mu\) about \(x\). If \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then \(|f_\mu(x)-f(x)|\leq L\mu\) for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compactly supported kernel smooths using only nearby function values; for an L-Lipschitz function, its approximation error is at most Lμ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_\mu(x)\) uses only \(f|_{\overline B(x,\mu)}\) and \(|f_\mu(x)-f(x)|\leq L\mu\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Additively smoothed objective and optimization problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a smoothed objective from a differentiable smooth baseline and an otherwise given smoothing term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q_1\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and let \(\widehat f:Q_1\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with
\[
\lVert\nabla\widehat f(x)-\nabla\widehat f(y)\rVert\le M\lVert x-y\rVert\qquad(x,y\in Q_1),
\]
for some \(M\ge0\). Given \(\mu>0\) and a smoothing term \(f_\mu:Q_1\to\mathbb R\), define
\[
\overline f_\mu(x):=\widehat f(x)+f_\mu(x),\qquad x\in Q_1.
\]
The corresponding smoothed problem is
\[
\min_{x\in Q_1}\overline f_\mu(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a differentiable baseline objective whose gradient is M-Lipschitz on Q1, a smoothing parameter μ>0 and a given smoothing term f_μ define the smoothed objective as their sum. The smoothed problem minimizes this sum over Q1.
assumptions_latex: \(\widehat f:Q_1\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and \(\nabla\widehat f\) is \(M\)-Lipschitz on \(Q_1\), with \(M\ge0\).
\(\mu>0\) and \(f_\mu:Q_1\to\mathbb R\) is a given smoothing term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline f_\mu=\widehat f+f_\mu\) on \(Q_1\), and the smoothed optimization problem is \(\min\{\overline f_\mu(x):x\in Q_1\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transfer of smoothed suboptimality to original-objective accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smoothing-gap certificate converting surrogate suboptimality into accuracy for the original objective. The parameter formula involving division by \(\ln n\) applies only when \(n>1\); the core implication needs only the displayed gap condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\ne\varnothing\), let \(n\in\mathbb N\), let \(\phi,\phi_\mu:Q\to\mathbb R\), and set \(\phi^*:=\inf_{y\in Q}\phi(y)\) and \(\phi_\mu^*:=\inf_{y\in Q}\phi_\mu(y)\). Suppose \(\mu>0\) and, for every \(y\in Q\), \[\phi_\mu(y)\le\phi(y)\le\phi_\mu(y)+\mu\ln n.\] If \(\epsilon>0\), \(\bar y\in Q\), \(\phi_\mu(\bar y)-\phi_\mu^*\le\epsilon/2\), and \(\mu\ln n\le\epsilon/2\), then \[\phi(\bar y)-\phi^*\le\epsilon.\] If \(n>1\), the choice \(\mu=\epsilon/(2\ln n)\) satisfies the gap condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the original objective lies between a smoothed objective and that smoothed objective plus mu log n, then epsilon-over-two surrogate suboptimality transfers to epsilon original suboptimality whenever the smoothing gap is at most epsilon over two. The stated explicit choice of mu is valid when n is greater than one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi(\bar y)-\phi^*\le\epsilon

knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing-Parameter Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value convergence, asymptotic optimality, and cluster-point optimality under uniformly vanishing bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed, let \(f,f_\mu:D\to\mathbb R\), and suppose \(f\) is lower semicontinuous with \(\inf_{x\in D}f(x)\in\mathbb R\). If \[b(\mu):=\sup_{x\in D}|f_\mu(x)-f(x)|\to0\qquad\text{as }\mu\downarrow0,\] then \[\left|\inf_{x\in D}f_\mu(x)-\inf_{x\in D}f(x)\right|\leq b(\mu)\to0.\] If \(x_\mu\in D\) and \(\varepsilon_\mu\geq0\) satisfy \[f_\mu(x_\mu)\leq\inf_{x\in D}f_\mu(x)+\varepsilon_\mu,\qquad \varepsilon_\mu\to0,\] then \[0\leq f(x_\mu)-\inf_{x\in D}f(x)\leq\varepsilon_\mu+2b(\mu)\to0.\] Moreover, if \(\mu_j\downarrow0\) and \(x_{\mu_j}\to\bar x\), then \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly vanishing bias makes the optimal values converge and makes increasingly accurate surrogate solutions asymptotically optimal for the target; every convergent subsequence of such solutions has a target minimizer as its limit.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and closed, \(f,f_\mu:D\to\mathbb R\), \(f\) is lower semicontinuous, and \(\inf_{x\in D}f(x)\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_\mu)-\inf_{x\in D}f(x)\to0\), \(\left|\inf_{x\in D}f_\mu(x)-\inf_{x\in D}f(x)\right|\to0\), and every convergent subsequence of \((x_\mu)\) has a target minimizer as its limit.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=|x|\) and \(f_\mu(x)=\sqrt{x^2+\mu^2}\) for \(x\in\mathbb R\) and \(\mu>0\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(D=\mathbb R\), let \(f(x)=0\) and \(f_k(x)=x^2/k\). For every fixed \(x\in\mathbb R\), \(f_k(x)\to0=f(x)\). Nevertheless, for every \(k\geq1\), \[\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}|f_k(x)-f(x)|=\infty.\] Thus pointwise convergence, even for smooth convex approximants, does not imply uniform approximation on a noncompact domain and cannot by itself furnish a finite uniform smoothing-gap certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth convex functions can converge pointwise on a noncompact domain while their worst-case approximation error remains infinite.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Failure of uniform convergence of \(f_k\) to \(f\) on \(D\) is certified by the existence of \(\varepsilon>0\), indices \(k_j\uparrow\infty\), and points \(x_j\in D\) such that \[|f_{k_j}(x_j)-f(x_j)|\geq\varepsilon\qquad\text{for every }j.\] If convergence is uniform on every compact subset of \(D\), then no subsequence of \((x_j)\) can lie in a common compact set. In a proper metric space this implies \((x_j)\) escapes every bounded subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonuniform convergence has moving witness points with errors bounded away from zero; under compact-uniform convergence, those points must escape compact sets.

children.top_down_role: Breakdown caused by approximation behavior over unbounded regions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_k\to f\) pointwise, but surrogate minimizers escape and their target values diverge.

notation.meaning: global minimizer of the kth surrogate

external source for this exact counterexample is missing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moving-well counterexample showing optimization failure under merely pointwise convergence on a noncompact domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(k\geq1\), set \[f_k(x):=x^2-(k^2+1)e^{-(x-k)^2},\qquad f(x):=x^2.\] Each \(f_k\) is continuous and coercive, hence has a global minimizer \(x_k\). For every fixed \(x\), \(f_k(x)\to f(x)\), while \(f_k(k)=-1\), so \(\inf f_k\leq-1\). On every bounded set, \(f_k\to f\) uniformly; consequently any sequence of global minimizers must escape every bounded set. Therefore \(f(x_k)=x_k^2\to\infty\), although \(\inf f=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative surrogate well moving to infinity preserves pointwise convergence but makes global surrogate minimizers escape and become arbitrarily poor for the target.
knowledge_statements.title: Noncompact-Domain Failure

knowledge_statements.title: Spurious Surrogate Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A uniformly convergent smooth surrogate can have stationary points converging to a nonstationary point of its limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) and, for \(\mu>0\), let \(f_\mu:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be defined by \(f(x)=x\) and \(f_\mu(x)=x+\mu\sin(x/\mu)\). Then \(\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}|f_\mu(x)-f(x)|\leq\mu\), so \(f_\mu\to f\) uniformly. Nevertheless, with \(x_\mu=\pi\mu\), one has \(f_\mu'(x_\mu)=1+\cos(\pi)=0\) and \(x_\mu\to0\), whereas \(f'(0)=1\neq0\). Thus accumulation points of stationary surrogate solutions need not be stationary for the limiting objective without gradient-consistency assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform function approximation alone does not preserve stationarity: stationary points of smooth surrogates can converge to a point where the limiting objective has nonzero derivative.

knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Violation Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite systems with inequality and equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constraint functions \(g_i:X\to\mathbb R\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(h_j:X\to\mathbb R\), \(j=1,\ldots,p\), representing \(g_i(x)\leq0\) and \(h_j(x)=0\), define the componentwise violation vector by \[v(x)=\bigl((g_1(x))_+,\ldots,(g_m(x))_+,|h_1(x)|,\ldots,|h_p(x)|\bigr),\qquad (t)_+=\max\{t,0\}.\] Every component of \(v(x)\) is nonnegative, and \(v(x)=0\) if and only if all represented constraints are satisfied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive parts measure individual inequality violations, while absolute values measure equality violations; the resulting vector vanishes exactly at feasible points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(x)=0\) if and only if \(g_i(x)\leq0\) for every \(i\) and \(h_j(x)=0\) for every \(j\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical finite-dimensional componentwise violation definition
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Max-Norm Violation Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Largest componentwise violation for a finite inequality-equality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty set, let \(m,p\) be nonnegative integers, and let \(g_i:X\to\mathbb R\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(h_j:X\to\mathbb R\), \(j=1,\ldots,p\), represent the constraints \(g_i(x)\leq0\) and \(h_j(x)=0\). For \(x\in X\), define \[V_\infty(x)=\max\left\{\max_{1\leq i\leq m}(g_i(x))_+,\;\max_{1\leq j\leq p}|h_j(x)|\right\},\qquad (t)_+=\max\{t,0\}.\] An inner maximum corresponding to an empty constraint family is omitted. Equivalently, \(V_\infty(x)=\|v(x)\|_\infty\), where \(v(x)\) is the componentwise violation vector. Hence \(V_\infty(x)\geq0\), and \(V_\infty(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\) satisfies every represented constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The max-norm violation measure is the largest individual inequality or equality violation and equals zero precisely when all represented constraints are satisfied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_\infty(x)=\|v(x)\|_\infty\), and \(V_\infty(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\) is feasible for the represented constraints.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct max-norm representation of finite componentwise constraint violations
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Distance Violation Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Violation measured geometrically against a nonempty feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(F\subset X\) be a nonempty feasible set. The set-distance violation measure is \[V_F(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,F):=\inf_{y\in F}d(x,y).\] It satisfies \(V_F(x)\geq0\) and is \(1\)-Lipschitz: \(|V_F(x)-V_F(z)|\leq d(x,z)\). Moreover, \(V_F(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\in\overline F\); consequently, when \(F\) is closed, its zero set is exactly \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to the feasible set is a nonnegative, one-Lipschitz violation measure whose zeros equal the feasible set when that set is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_F(x)=0\iff x\in\overline F\), and if \(F\) is closed then \(V_F^{-1}(0)=F\).

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical exterior penalty for finite inequality-equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the constrained problem with objective \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), inequalities \(g_i(x)\leq0\), and equalities \(h_j(x)=0\), the quadratic exterior penalty with parameter \(\rho>0\) is \[P_\rho(x)=f(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}(g_i(x))_+^2+\sum_{j=1}^{p}h_j(x)^2\right).\] The added term is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at feasible points. Feasibility is ordinarily approached by solving a sequence with \(\rho\to\infty\); finite-parameter exactness is not generally guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic penalty adds squared equality and positive-part inequality violations to the objective, usually requiring the penalty parameter to diverge for feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_\rho(x)=f(x)\) at feasible points, while \(P_\rho(x)>f(x)\) whenever at least one constraint is violated.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Power Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exterior penalties generated by positive powers of componentwise violations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty set, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(g_i:X\to\mathbb R\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and \(h_j:X\to\mathbb R\), \(j=1,\ldots,p\), represent the constraints \(g_i(x)\leq0\) and \(h_j(x)=0\). For \(q>0\) and \(\rho>0\), define \[P_{\rho,q}(x)=f(x)+\rho\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}(g_i(x))_+^q+\sum_{j=1}^{p}|h_j(x)|^q\right).\] The penalty term vanishes exactly when all represented constraints are satisfied. The case \(q=1\) is a linear, generally nonsmooth violation penalty, while \(q=2\) is a quadratic penalty up to the parameter convention. If \(q>1\) and the constraint functions are continuously differentiable, the penalty term is continuously differentiable at feasible points, but finite-parameter exactness is not guaranteed merely by choosing \(q>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A power penalty sums positive powers of the individual violations. Exponent one gives a generally nonsmooth linear penalty, while exponents above one can give a continuously differentiable but not necessarily exact penalty.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i:X\to\mathbb R\) and \(h_j:X\to\mathbb R\) represent the finite constraint system
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\rho,q}(x)-f(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\) satisfies every represented constraint.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Nonexact Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite smooth penalties may shift minimizers away from feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R}x\) subject to \(x=0\). For every finite \(\rho>0\), the smooth quadratic penalty is \[P_\rho(x)=x+\frac{\rho}{2}x^2.\] Its unique stationary point and global minimizer is \(x_\rho=-1/\rho\), which is infeasible, although \(x_\rho\to0\) as \(\rho\to\infty\). Thus a smooth penalty whose derivative with respect to violation vanishes at zero need not reproduce the constrained solution for any finite penalty parameter; exactness typically requires a nonsmooth first-order growth term or additional structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth quadratic penalty can have only infeasible minimizers for every finite parameter, even though those minimizers converge to feasibility as the parameter diverges.
assumptions_latex: The constrained problem is \(\min x\) subject to \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R}P_\rho(x)=\{-1/\rho\}\not\subset\{0\}\) for every finite \(\rho\).

knowledge_statements.title: ℓ1 Constraint-Violation Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsmooth linear aggregation of finite constraint violations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For objective \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), inequalities \(g_i(x)\leq0\), and equalities \(h_j(x)=0\), the \(\ell_1\) constraint-violation penalty is \[P_\rho^{(1)}(x)=f(x)+\rho\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}(g_i(x))_++\sum_{j=1}^{p}|h_j(x)|\right),\qquad \rho>0.\] The penalty term equals \(\rho\|v(x)\|_1\), where \(v(x)\) is the componentwise violation vector. Its linear growth away from feasibility permits finite-parameter exactness under suitable constraint qualifications, multiplier bounds, or error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ℓ1 penalty adds the sum of individual violations and can recover constrained minimizers at a finite penalty parameter under suitable regularity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_\rho^{(1)}(x)=f(x)+\rho\|v(x)\|_1\), with \(\|v(x)\|_1=0\) exactly at feasible points.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Violation Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsmooth penalty based on the single largest constraint violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For inequalities \(g_i(x)\leq0\) and equalities \(h_j(x)=0\), define the maximum-violation penalty by \[P_\rho^{(\infty)}(x)=f(x)+\rho\max\left\{\max_{1\leq i\leq m}(g_i(x))_+,\;\max_{1\leq j\leq p}|h_j(x)|\right\},\qquad \rho>0.\] Equivalently, \(P_\rho^{(\infty)}(x)=f(x)+\rho\|v(x)\|_\infty\). The added term is nonnegative, vanishes exactly on the feasible set, and has linear growth in the largest componentwise violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This penalty adds the largest individual constraint violation to the objective and grows linearly away from feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_\rho^{(\infty)}(x)=f(x)+\rho\|v(x)\|_\infty\), and the added term vanishes exactly at feasible points.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Distance Exact Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear distance penalty for a closed feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(F\subset X\) be nonempty and closed, and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\). The set-distance penalty with parameter \(\rho>0\) is \[P_\rho(x)=f(x)+\rho\operatorname{dist}(x,F).\] It is called exact at a constrained local minimizer \(x^*\in F\) if some \(\bar\rho<\infty\) and neighborhood \(U\) of \(x^*\) satisfy \(P_\rho(x^*)\leq P_\rho(x)\) for every \(x\in U\) and every \(\rho\geq\bar\rho\). Global exactness is defined by taking \(U=X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-distance exact penalty adds distance to the feasible set and is exact when all sufficiently large finite parameters preserve the constrained minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactness at \(x^*\) means \(\exists\bar\rho<\infty\) such that \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in U}P_\rho(x)\) for every \(\rho\geq\bar\rho\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of local and global finite-parameter exactness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Distance Function and Associated Nonsmooth Exact Penalty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminological definition from the source; it does not independently establish a finite exactness threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex function h:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R} with h(0)=0 is called a strong distance function if there exists \delta>0 such that h(c)\geq\delta\lVert c\rVert_1 for every c\in\mathbb{R}^m. For such h, \sigma>0, and the constraint-violation map c^{(-)}, the associated nonsmooth exact penalty function is P_{\sigma,h}(x)=f(x)+\sigma h(c^{(-)}(x)).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong distance function is a convex function vanishing at zero that uniformly dominates a positive multiple of the l1 norm. The source calls the resulting violation-penalized objective a nonsmooth exact penalty function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{\sigma,h}(x):=f(x)+\sigma h(c^{(-)}(x))\text{ is termed the associated nonsmooth exact penalty function.}

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound-Based Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local exactness from objective Lipschitz continuity and a constraint error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(F\subset X\) be closed, and let \(x^*\in F\) locally minimize \(f\) over \(F\). Suppose on a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x^*\), the function \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and a violation measure \(V\geq0\) satisfies \(V^{-1}(0)=F\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(x,F)\leq\kappa V(x)\). Then every \(\rho>L\kappa\) makes \(x^*\) a local minimizer of \(P_\rho(x)=f(x)+\rho V(x)\). Thus the error-bound modulus and objective Lipschitz modulus give the exactness threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local error bound converts violation into distance, making a linear penalty exact whenever its parameter exceeds the Lipschitz constant times the error-bound modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(x^*\) locally minimizes \(f\) over the closed set \(F\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\rho>L\kappa\), \(x^*\) locally minimizes \(P_\rho=f+\rho V\).

knowledge_statements.title: Calmness-Based Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global linear-penalty exactness derived from calmness below of the perturbation value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_\rho(x):=f(x)+\rho g(x)\). If \(v(t)\ge v(0)-Lt\) for all \(t\ge0\), then every \(\rho>L\) satisfies \[\inf_{x\in X}P_\rho(x)=v(0).\] Moreover, every minimizer of \(P_\rho\) is feasible and minimizes \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the perturbation value can decrease by at most L per unit violation, every penalty weight larger than L preserves the constrained value and makes all attained penalized minimizers constrained-optimal.
assumptions_latex: \(v(t):=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ g(x)\le t\}\) satisfies \(v(t)\ge v(0)-Lt\) for every \(t\ge0\), for some \(L\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\rho>L\), \(\inf_{x\in X}P_\rho(x)=v(0)\), and every minimizer of \(P_\rho\) belongs to \(C\) and minimizes \(f\) over \(C\).

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Nonlinear Programming-Based Value Functions p. 254

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\rho\ge0\), the penalized value admits the scalar representation \[\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(f(x)+\rho g(x)\bigr)=\inf_{t\ge0}\bigl(v(t)+\rho t\bigr).\] Therefore its value equals the constrained value \(v(0)\) if and only if \(v(t)+\rho t\ge v(0)\) for all \(t\ge0\). If the inequality is strict for every \(t>0\), any attained penalized minimum must have zero violation and is consequently a constrained minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The penalized problem reduces to minimizing the perturbed value plus a linear charge; exactness is equivalent to this scalar expression being minimized at zero violation.
